paragraphs: This paper develops a mathematical way to study when generative AI can improve human work. It represents jobs, workers, and the match between them, then divides skills into decision-level and action-level components. That division lets the model describe complementary abilities more precisely than a single overall measure of worker skill.

The analysis examines how changes in these component abilities affect the probability of completing a job successfully. It identifies conditions under which improvements produce sharp changes in success probability. It also establishes sufficient conditions for combining workers with complementary abilities to substantially outperform a single worker; those conditions describe when the advantage follows, rather than claiming that collaboration always helps.

The framework explains productivity compression: assistance can give larger gains to workers who initially have lower skill levels. The authors connect the model to O*NET and Big-Bench Lite data using methods that divide skills into subskills. This demonstrates a practical route for studying which combinations of human and AI abilities support better job performance.
icml-2025-a-mathematical-framework-for-a.tldr: A mathematical model identifies conditions under which complementary human and AI subskills improve job success.

paragraphs: This paper studies how limited training data causes overfitting when pairwise energy-based models are used to infer interaction networks. It starts with a Gaussian model, where learning can be separated into independently evolving components associated with the coupling matrix. This makes it possible to analyze how different parts of the model change during training.

The analysis connects their learning timescales to the spectral structure of the empirical covariance matrix. Useful early-stopping points emerge from the interaction between these timescales and the model’s initial state. Using asymptotic random matrix theory, the authors also model corrections caused by finite data and develop an energy-based counterpart to generalized cross-validation.

The framework extends with small changes to pairwise maximum-entropy models with binary variables. It suggests empirical shrinkage corrections as a way to manage overfitting in discrete models. For broader energy-based models, the authors propose a further generalization by deriving score-function dynamics under score matching through the neural tangent kernel. That final step expands the analytical direction beyond the initial testbed.
icml-2025-a-theoretical-framework-for-ov.tldr: An analysis of learning timescales explains overfitting in pairwise energy-based models and motivates early stopping and shrinkage corrections.

paragraphs: Graph neural networks can classify nodes effectively while remaining vulnerable to small adversarial changes in their inputs. Adversarial training helps, but its success leaves a theoretical question: how well does robustness learned during training carry over to other examples? This paper develops a high-probability bound on that generalization gap.

The authors use covering number analysis, which describes model complexity through a collection of representatives covering possible behaviors. Their construction accounts for the entire perturbed feature matrix by first covering the set of allowed perturbations. This provides a way to include adversarial changes directly in the complexity analysis used to bound generalization.

The result applies to a range of graph neural networks. Applying it to several popular architectures reveals architecture-related factors that influence the gap between training and generalization performance under attack. Experiments on benchmark datasets provide evidence consistent with the theory. The contribution is therefore both a general analytical tool and an explanation of how architecture can affect robust generalization.
icml-2025-adversarial-robust-generalizat.tldr: A covering-number analysis bounds adversarial generalization in graph neural networks and identifies architecture-related influences on the generalization gap.

paragraphs: Adding generated audio to generated video creates quality problems involving both individual sounds and their agreement with the visuals. Existing assessment methods struggle with unrealistic or inconsistent content of this kind. This paper introduces a dataset and a multimodal rating model designed to evaluate these issues and help choose among candidate outputs.

The dataset, AGAVQA-3k, contains 3,382 audio-visual examples produced by 16 video-to-audio methods. One subset supplies scores for audio quality, content consistency, and overall quality. Another supports selection between pairs of outputs. These complementary tasks distinguish assigning a quality score from deciding which candidate should be presented to a user.

AGAV-Rater adapts a large multimodal model to perform multidimensional scoring and candidate selection. It also evaluates audio and music generated from text. The authors report state-of-the-art results on their dataset and on text-to-audio and text-to-music datasets. Subjective tests further support improvements in video-to-audio performance and user experience, connecting assessment accuracy to the usefulness of the selected content.
icml-2025-agav-rater-adapting-large-mult.tldr: AGAV-Rater scores generated audio-visual content across quality dimensions and selects preferred outputs, supported by a new evaluation dataset.

paragraphs: AutoAdvExBench tests whether language-model agents can autonomously find ways around defenses against adversarial examples. Its tasks reflect work performed by machine learning security researchers. The intended value is practical: solving these challenges could make agents useful for evaluating defenses, rather than merely demonstrating success on loosely related security exercises.

The benchmark distinguishes exercise-style defenses from real-world defenses, and the results show a substantial difficulty gap. The strongest agent ensemble breaks 87% of the exercise-style defenses but only 37% of the real-world ones. Performance on simplified challenges therefore gives an incomplete picture of the agents’ ability to handle actual defense implementations.

The difference also affects comparisons between models. Claude Sonnet 3.5 and Opus 4 achieve similar exercise-style success rates, at 75% and 79%, while their real-world rates differ substantially, at 13% and 30%. These findings make the benchmark’s task composition consequential: evaluations using realistic defenses reveal capability differences that exercise-style tests can largely obscure.
icml-2025-autoadvexbench-benchmarking-au.tldr: AutoAdvExBench finds that success against exercise-style adversarial defenses does not reliably reflect success against real-world defenses.

paragraphs: AutoElicit uses knowledge from language models to help train predictive models when labeled examples are scarce. The motivation is that interpretable models remain valuable in areas such as healthcare, biology, and finance, while using a language model directly can introduce cost, complexity, and transparency concerns. The method transfers knowledge through prior distributions over model parameters.

In Bayesian learning, those priors express information available before incorporating the labeled data. AutoElicit constructs informative priors from language models and allows them to be refined through natural-language instructions. This offers a way to bring domain knowledge into a smaller predictive model without requiring the usual time-consuming process of eliciting priors from experts.

The authors compare AutoElicit with uninformative priors and with in-context learning, and study how to select between the two language-model-based approaches. Their results show reduced prediction error with fewer labels and consistent advantages over in-context learning in the study. For a urinary-tract-infection predictor using sensor recordings from people living with dementia, they report saving more than six months of labeling effort.
icml-2025-autoelicit-using-large-languag.tldr: AutoElicit converts language-model knowledge into adjustable Bayesian priors that improve predictive learning with fewer labeled examples.

paragraphs: CtrlSynth addresses a problem in training vision-language models: large image-text datasets can contain noise, mismatched pairs, and uneven coverage. Synthetic data can help, but generating useful variety requires control over what changes. The paper introduces a pipeline that supports fine-grained manipulation when synthesizing either images or text.

The pipeline breaks an image’s visual meaning into basic elements. Users specify policies that add, remove, or replace elements, and pretrained foundation models reason about and recombine them into natural, varied samples. This decomposition makes control explicit at the level of content, instead of leaving the entire synthesis process to an undirected generation request.

CtrlSynth is described as modular, closed-loop, and training-free, allowing different pretrained language or diffusion models to support synthesis. The authors evaluate its use across 31 datasets covering vision and vision-language tasks. They report substantial improvements in CLIP’s zero-shot classification, image-text retrieval, and compositional reasoning. These results connect control over generated content to better use of synthetic data for multimodal learning.
icml-2025-ctrlsynth-controllable-image-t.tldr: CtrlSynth improves multimodal learning by generating images and text through controllable edits to basic visual-semantic elements.

paragraphs: Maximum entropy reinforcement learning encourages exploration alongside reward seeking. Conventional Gaussian policies restrict the distributions of actions a policy can represent. Diffusion policies offer greater flexibility, but their marginal entropy is difficult to compute, creating an obstacle to using them within the maximum entropy objective.

DIME addresses that obstacle using approximate inference methods for diffusion models. The authors derive a lower bound on the maximum entropy objective, providing a tractable basis for learning expressive policies. They also introduce a policy iteration scheme and prove that it converges to the optimal diffusion policy. The guarantee concerns that policy setting, rather than unrestricted optimality across every possible policy representation.

On challenging high-dimensional control benchmarks, DIME substantially outperforms other diffusion-based methods. It is also competitive with leading methods that do not use diffusion, while requiring fewer algorithmic design choices and smaller update-to-data ratios. Together, these findings support diffusion policies as a practical way to expand policy expressiveness while retaining the exploration rationale of maximum entropy learning.
icml-2025-dime-diffusion-based-maximum-e.tldr: DIME uses a lower-bound objective to combine expressive diffusion policies with maximum entropy reinforcement learning.

paragraphs: Cognitive scientists use symbolic models to express precise hypotheses about learning and decision-making. Finding a model that explains observed behavior usually requires substantial scientific effort. This paper adapts FunSearch, which combines language models with an evolutionary algorithm, to automatically search for programs that describe human and animal behavior.

The authors apply the approach to datasets from three species performing a classic reward-learning task. The resulting programs outperform state-of-the-art cognitive models for each species in the study. The task already has a substantial modeling history, so the comparison tests whether automated program discovery can add useful candidates in an established area of cognitive research.

The discovered programs are interpretable as symbolic learning and decision-making algorithms. Their value therefore extends beyond fitting behavior: researchers can read them as proposed explanations of the processes generating that behavior. The results support language-model-powered program synthesis as a tool for proposing scientific hypotheses. Those programs remain hypotheses about cognition; their predictive performance does not itself establish that brains implement the discovered algorithms.
icml-2025-discovering-symbolic-cognitive.tldr: An adaptation of FunSearch discovers interpretable cognitive programs that outperform established models on reward-learning data from three species.

paragraphs: Conference submission limits can affect authors who have not themselves exceeded the limit because papers are shared across coauthors. This paper formalizes that fairness problem for desk rejection. Within its formulation, it identifies an impossibility when the number of authors exceeds three: rejecting papers solely for excessive submissions cannot avoid harming innocent authors.

The authors explain how this can disadvantage early-career researchers whose coauthors have much larger submission counts. They propose choosing desk rejections through a fairness-aware optimization mechanism. Two objectives make fairness explicit: worst-case fairness and average fairness. These provide different ways to assess how the consequences of rejection are distributed across affected authors.

The computational results distinguish those objectives sharply. Optimizing worst-case fairness is NP-hard, while average fairness can be optimized efficiently with linear programming. Case studies show greater equity than existing practices, including those used at CVPR 2025. The framework makes both the collateral effects of submission limits and the computational tradeoffs of fairer rejection policies available for formal analysis.
icml-2025-dissecting-submission-limit-in.tldr: A formal analysis exposes fairness problems in submission-limit desk rejections and proposes an efficiently optimizable average-fairness alternative.

paragraphs: Representing an object boundary as a polygon can be efficient, but training a model to predict its vertices is difficult. One problem is deciding how predicted boundary points should correspond to target points. This paper introduces a vertex regression loss based on elliptical Fourier descriptors to address that optimization challenge.

The loss compares boundaries through their frequency-domain representation, resolving ambiguities in boundary point assignment. It avoids the need to rasterize polygons or use heuristic approximations during this matching process. The associated EFDTR framework is trained end to end and uses Fourier-based representations to capture object contours.

EFDTR separates contour prediction into two stages. The first predicts elliptical Fourier descriptors to establish the overall shape; the second refines the contour for finer accuracy. On COCO, it outperforms existing polygon-based methods. The result supports polygon representations as a promising alternative for instance segmentation, while the stated comparison establishes an advantage over polygon-based competitors rather than a general superiority over pixel-based approaches.
icml-2025-efdtr-learnable-elliptical-fou.tldr: EFDTR uses Fourier-based boundary matching and two-stage contour prediction to improve polygon-based instance segmentation.

paragraphs: Generating three-dimensional molecular conformers accurately and quickly is useful for computational chemistry and drug discovery. Existing diffusion and flow-based generators can require substantial computation both during training and when producing samples. This paper addresses those two costs separately within a flow-matching approach.

For training, the authors introduce an SO(3)-Averaged Flow objective. They report that it converges faster and reaches better generation quality than conditional optimal transport flow or Kabsch-aligned flow. Models trained with the new objective can reach state-of-the-art conformer generation quality, making training efficiency compatible with strong output quality in the reported results.

For inference, the paper applies reflow and distillation methods to enable generation in only a few steps, or even one step, while retaining high quality. This tackles the repeated computation involved in sampling separately from the cost of learning the model. Together, the two mechanisms show a path toward more efficient flow-based conformer generation across both stages of use.
icml-2025-efficient-molecular-conformer-.tldr: An SO(3)-Averaged Flow objective accelerates conformer-model training, while reflow and distillation enable high-quality few-step or one-step generation.

paragraphs: Three-dimensional vision-language grounding has far fewer labeled scenes available than two-dimensional models have training images. LIFT-GS addresses this bottleneck by transferring supervision from established 2D foundation models into a 3D system. It uses rendered views as the connection between the two settings, without requiring 3D annotations for that supervision.

Starting from point clouds, LIFT-GS predicts 3D Gaussian representations and language-conditioned 3D masks. Differentiable rendering turns those masks into 2D views, where SAM, CLIP, and LLaMA provide supervision. Because training signals pass through the rendering process, the approach supports end-to-end learning of complete encoder-decoder architectures and is described as model-agnostic.

The authors report 25.7% mAP for open-vocabulary instance segmentation, compared with a previous best of 20.2%, alongside consistent 10–30% improvements on referential grounding tasks. They also report a pretraining benefit equivalent to doubling fine-tuning datasets. These scaling results suggest that limited data remains a major constraint on 3D grounding, and that rendered supervision can help address it.
icml-2025-from-thousands-to-billions-3d-.tldr: LIFT-GS transfers 2D foundation-model supervision through differentiable rendering to improve 3D language grounding without 3D annotations.

paragraphs: This paper studies the solutions gradient descent approaches through training itself, a phenomenon called implicit bias. Its focus is non-homogeneous deep networks trained with exponential loss, extending analysis beyond the homogeneous networks emphasized in prior work. The results concern long-run behavior under a near-homogeneity condition.

The analysis requires starting from sufficiently small empirical risk, with the threshold determined by a measure of the network’s non-homogeneity. From such a starting point, a normalized margin increases nearly monotonically. Meanwhile, the parameter norm grows without bound, but the direction of the parameter vector converges. Thus, increasing parameter magnitude can coexist with a stable limiting direction.

The limiting direction satisfies the Karush–Kuhn–Tucker conditions for a margin maximization problem. This is a precise constrained-optimization characterization, rather than a claim that every run reaches a global maximum. The covered network class includes residual connections and non-homogeneous activation functions. These extensions make the theory applicable to structures outside the homogeneous setting while retaining explicit conditions on when its conclusions hold.
icml-2025-implicit-bias-of-gradient-desc.tldr: Under near-homogeneity and sufficiently low initial risk, gradient descent converges in direction toward a KKT point of a margin maximization problem.

paragraphs: Safety filters use uncertainty estimates to restrict a controller’s available actions. When uncertainty is very large, those restrictions can become infeasible: no input satisfies the filter’s constraints. This paper addresses that situation by collecting additional data during operation, rather than assuming that a safe backup controller is available.

The method combines a learned model with a control barrier function to construct a robust safety certificate. When feasible, that certificate ensures safety. When infeasibility occurs, a Gaussian-process bandit-type algorithm explores, guided by the barrier function so that the additional data contributes toward the safety of the closed-loop system.

This integration makes exploration part of the response to uncertainty that prevents the filter from operating. The authors prove safety in a general setting without requiring a prior model or backup controller, provided the true system belongs to a reproducing kernel Hilbert space. That function-space assumption is part of the guarantee: the result supports safe learning under the specified setting, rather than unconditional safety for arbitrary unknown systems.
icml-2025-learning-safe-control-via-on-t.tldr: Barrier-guided bandit exploration restores useful safety information when uncertainty makes a control filter infeasible, with guarantees under an RKHS assumption.

paragraphs: Detecting unusual whole graphs is difficult when training data contains only normal examples or very few anomalies. AGDiff addresses this shortage by generating artificial anomalous graphs for training. The goal is to give a detector examples of departures from normality instead of relying solely on a model of normal graphs.

AGDiff uses latent diffusion to introduce subtle perturbations into graph representations. The resulting pseudo-anomalous graphs closely resemble normal ones, providing examples that require a finer distinction than obviously different graphs would. A classifier is trained jointly to separate normal graphs from these generated anomalies, producing more discriminative decision boundaries.

The paper reports that this explicit generation-and-discrimination approach can identify complex anomalous patterns that other approaches might overlook. Across its experiments, AGDiff significantly outperforms several state-of-the-art graph-level anomaly detection baselines. The stated findings support using diffusion as a source of informative abnormal training examples, expanding its role beyond learning the distribution of normal data.
icml-2025-leveraging-diffusion-model-as-.tldr: AGDiff generates subtle pseudo-anomalous graphs with latent diffusion and jointly trains a classifier to improve graph-level anomaly detection.

paragraphs: Thinning summarizes a dataset by selecting a small collection of representative points. Existing sub-Gaussian thinning algorithms can match uniform subsampling quality with substantially fewer points, but their theoretical guarantees have restricted coverage and pessimistic dependence on dimension. This paper develops a low-rank analysis to broaden and sharpen those guarantees.

The analysis applies to any distribution and any kernel. Its high-quality compression guarantee depends on the kernel or data matrix being approximately low-rank, meaning that a lower-dimensional structure captures much of the relevant matrix information. The broad scope of the analysis therefore comes with a meaningful structural condition for the strongest compression conclusion.

The authors also design practical thinning approaches for several computational tasks. These improve the best known guarantees for approximating transformer attention, accelerating stochastic-gradient training through reordering, and distinguishing distributions in near-linear time. The contribution connects representative data selection to these different settings through a shared analysis of low-rank structure, rather than treating each application as an unrelated compression problem.
icml-2025-low-rank-thinning-aeb577ab48.tldr: A low-rank analysis broadens thinning guarantees and improves theoretical results for attention approximation, training reordering, and distribution comparison.

paragraphs: A matrix of pairwise distances can violate metric rules because of noise, missing entries, or inconsistent data. The metric nearness problem seeks a nearby matrix that obeys those rules. A major computational obstacle is the cubic number of triangle-inequality constraints, which makes direct treatment expensive for large matrices.

MetricEmbedding uses a tropical inner product, based on max-plus operations, to construct its solution. The authors prove a triangle-inequality property for non-negative real matrices and turn the repair problem into continuous optimization that minimizes distance to the target matrix. This embeds metric structure into the proposed representation rather than handling the full constraint collection directly.

The method also produces metric-preserving embeddings, supporting real-time updates and reducing downstream computation and storage. Experiments report speed improvements of up to 60 times over state-of-the-art approaches, alongside substantially lower memory use. The method scales across matrices from 10,000 by 10,000 to 100,000 by 100,000, demonstrating the practical importance of changing how metric compliance is represented.
icml-2025-metricembedding-accelerate-met.tldr: MetricEmbedding uses a tropical-inner-product formulation to repair distance matrices efficiently while producing metric-preserving embeddings.

paragraphs: Open-ended detection locates objects and generates category names freely, without requiring an additional vocabulary at inference. Open-Det targets the training cost and slow convergence of existing systems for this task. Its design coordinates object localization, name generation, vision-language alignment, and transfer of knowledge from a vision-language model.

The framework reconstructs the object detector and name generator to accelerate their training. A bidirectional aligner connects visual and language representations, while a prompt distiller transfers vision-language-model knowledge into prompts used for naming objects. A masked alignment loss removes contradictory supervision, and a joint loss strengthens classification. These components address both representation alignment and the training signals used to learn it.

Compared with GenerateU, Open-Det uses 0.077 million training examples versus 5.077 million and 31 epochs versus 149. It also uses four V100 GPUs rather than sixteen A100s while reporting an APr improvement of 1.0%. This comparison supports the framework’s stated advantage in training efficiency alongside higher detection performance.
icml-2025-open-det-an-efficient-learning.tldr: Open-Det combines improved detection, name generation, alignment, and distillation to outperform GenerateU with substantially fewer training resources.

paragraphs: Learning guarantees for changing multiplayer games can become uninformative when payoffs vary substantially. Yet large changes need not be hard to anticipate. This paper introduces a framework that explicitly accounts for agents’ ability to forecast the underlying state of nature that determines future payoffs.

The proposed POMWU algorithm extends optimistic Multiplicative Weight Update with context. Agents predict the state online and use those predictions to adapt their strategies. This makes forecast accuracy part of the learning analysis, allowing the framework to distinguish unpredictable variation from changes that agents can usefully anticipate.

The authors establish guarantees for social welfare and convergence to equilibrium. When prediction errors are bounded, the framework achieves performance comparable to the static setting, despite the game changing over time. That conclusion depends on prediction quality, rather than holding for arbitrary forecasts. A traffic-routing experiment provides empirical evidence of POMWU’s effectiveness. Together, the theory and experiment support evaluating learning in changing games through predictability as well as through the magnitude of change.
icml-2025-prediction-aware-learning-in-m.tldr: POMWU incorporates forecasts into learning in changing games and obtains static-like guarantees when prediction errors are bounded.

paragraphs: Graph-level anomaly detection must often learn from normal graphs because examples of abnormal graphs are scarce or unavailable. Self-Discriminative Modeling addresses this by training a neural network to create its own pseudo-anomalies while also learning to recognize them. The entire training process uses normal graphs as its starting data.

The two learning tasks are coupled: constructing artificial anomalies supplies examples for the detector, and discrimination is integrated with that construction. The paper describes the generated graphs as interpolating between normal and real anomalous graphs. This relationship helps establish a reliable decision boundary, making the character of the synthetic examples central to the approach.

The authors develop three variants with different computational efficiency and stability properties. Across 12 graph benchmarks, all three consistently outperform state-of-the-art graph-level anomaly detection baselines. They attribute this success to combining a discriminative classifier with well-posed pseudo-anomalies. The results support joint generation and detection as a way to learn useful boundaries without requiring anomalous graphs in the training set.
icml-2025-self-discriminative-modeling-f.tldr: Self-Discriminative Modeling jointly creates pseudo-anomalous graphs and learns to detect them using only normal training graphs.

paragraphs: This paper studies clustering defined by two weighted graphs over the same vertices. A candidate split cuts edges in both graphs, and the objective is to minimize the ratio of the cut weight in the first graph to that in the second. The second graph therefore changes how the quality of a partition is judged.

The authors establish a Cheeger-type inequality connecting the best constrained clustering solution with spectral properties of the two graphs. Such a connection makes matrix-based calculations relevant to the partitioning objective. They use the signed Laplacian of the second graph to reduce computational complexity while maintaining accuracy.

The resulting algorithm solves a generalized eigenvalue problem to obtain a clustering solution. Experiments on synthetic and real-world datasets demonstrate practical effectiveness, with notable improvements in difficult settings where traditional spectral clustering struggles. The paper’s contribution combines a theoretical relationship between cuts and spectra with a computational formulation intended to make constrained clustering more effective.
icml-2025-signed-laplacians-for-constrai.tldr: A Cheeger-type inequality and signed-Laplacian formulation support an efficient spectral algorithm for constrained graph clustering.

paragraphs: This paper examines follow-the-regularized-leader learning when random shocks continually affect payoff observations and strategy updates. In the studied dynamics, randomness pushes play toward pure strategies, where a player concentrates on one action. Every player reaches arbitrarily small neighborhoods of pure strategies in finite time and revisits such neighborhoods infinitely often.

Approaching a pure strategy does not mean eventually staying there. The authors show that if the dynamics have a limit, it must be a pure Nash equilibrium. They also characterize stable attracting spans of pure strategies: these occur exactly when the span is closed under better replies. This links persistent behavior under uncertainty to the availability of payoff-improving responses.

The paper further studies games whose deterministic learning dynamics recur, including zero-sum games with interior equilibria. Randomness disrupts that recurrence and produces an average drift toward the boundary. These results distinguish repeated movement toward extreme strategies from actual convergence, while explaining how uncertainty changes the long-run structure of regularized learning.
icml-2025-the-impact-of-uncertainty-on-r.tldr: Randomly perturbed FTRL repeatedly approaches pure strategies, with pure Nash equilibria as its only possible limits.

paragraphs: Visual reprogramming adapts CLIP by adding a trainable pattern to input images. Existing approaches learn one pattern from descriptions of all downstream classes. The paper argues that this limited capacity can miss varied descriptive attributes, such as shape or texture, and may emphasize attributes that provide little help in distinguishing classes.

The proposed method divides the descriptions into groups and trains separate visual prompts for them. Groups can be formed using explicit causes or unsupervised clustering. A probabilistic reweighting matrix then combines the prompts’ outputs according to their contributions to each class. This allows different prompts to contribute differently to a classification decision.

The theoretical analysis shows that decoupled visual prompts lower an empirical risk bound. Experiments report better average performance than baselines across 11 downstream datasets, without claiming improvement on every dataset. The reweighting mechanism also provides a way to inspect how individual prompts influence predictions. The framework therefore connects a more differentiated adaptation method with a probabilistic account of its classification decisions.
icml-2025-understanding-model-reprogramm.tldr: Separately trained visual prompts and class-specific probabilistic reweighting improve CLIP reprogramming on average while exposing each prompt’s contribution.

paragraphs: Deep models for tabular data can perform well when training and evaluation data share a distribution, yet struggle as that distribution changes over time. This paper examines two sources of the problem: how data is divided for training and validation, and whether learned representations retain useful trends and periodic patterns.

The authors find that even a random split can substantially improve performance over commonly used temporally ordered splits in their investigation. Their proposed splitting protocol addresses training lag and validation bias to improve generalization across multiple methods. This makes the training protocol itself an important part of understanding performance under temporal shift.

The representation analysis also finds that deep tabular models often fail to capture important temporal structure. To address that gap, the authors introduce a plug-and-play temporal embedding based on Fourier series expansion. It learns and incorporates temporal patterns into existing methods. Experiments show that combining the embedding with the improved splitting strategy produces more effective and robust learning from temporal tabular data.
icml-2025-understanding-the-limits-of-de.tldr: Improved data splitting and a Fourier-based temporal embedding help deep tabular models handle changing trends and periodic patterns.
